source.title: Why Linear Interpretability Works: Invariant Subspaces as a Result of Architectural Constraints
source.authors: A. Saurez; You-Sung Lee; Dong-Soo Har

record.tranche_reason: The paper applies feature-direction and SAE analyses to LLM representations and reports results on those settings; it does not reproduce the original toy-model experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper's main measured results are SAE classification accuracies and SAE-feature overlap between class tokens and instances. It also reports a modular-division experiment and a polysemy comparison; those findings do not test the listed versions as framed. Theoretical arguments and cited findings are not recorded as empirical result rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs on attention-head outputs of four LLMs and reports whether their sparse latents recover semantic class structure. That bears weakly on the V4 claim that LLMs contain sparse features a dictionary can recover. Two kinds of evidence are relevant: class classification from SAE latents (Table 2) and top-32 SAE latent overlap between class tokens and instances (Fig. 4). The study does not reproduce the toy models. Its capacity (Prop. 3.8) and one-dimensionality (Prop. B.2) arguments are theoretical only.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors argue that linear interfaces (OV circuits, unembedding) force communicable features into context-invariant subspaces. They argue that tokens supply those directions (Self-Reference Property), and that zero-shot, unsupervised and SAE probes recover the same directional structure across eight tasks and four model families. They conclude that transformers are interpretable by design. They acknowledge not covering nonlinear (QK) features or when subspaces are 1-D.
record.recipe_differences: The study advances an architectural account and evaluates semantic directions and SAE latents in transformer models; it does not reproduce the original toy-model setup or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported SAE classification varies across model families and task datasets; the paper also reports different outcomes for linear and MLP readout settings in modular division.

fits_no_version.finding: In a 2-layer transformer trained on modular division with an MLP head, accuracy was ~95% while a linear probe reached ~20% and no Fourier circle formed. Seeds that did form Fourier structure had successful linear probes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear readout interfaces, not training dynamics alone, constrain representations to linear or Fourier structure.

fits_no_version.finding: For Fruits plus Companies, a single shared 'Apple' token and separate domain tokens gave similar classification accuracy (69% vs 65.7%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A polysemous token's senses are linearly separable directions modulated by context (token-level polysemy, not neuron polysemanticity).

fits_no_version.finding: In LLaMA3-8B, most attention heads show class-token cosine similarity higher with same-class instances than with other-class instances (Fig. 3: 86.0–97.6% of heads; the text says 89.6–98.6%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Token hidden states give context-invariant directions for their semantic class (linear representation / self-reference).

record.problems: Table 2 reports only the single best-performing (top-1) attention head per method and task; the paper gives no uncertainty estimates or chance-level baselines for these accuracies. The theoretical discussion acknowledges that it does not determine when invariant subspaces are one-dimensional versus higher-dimensional.

untested.parts: No toy sparse-feature networks, sparsity-dependent transition, or geometry of superposed features.
Prop. 3.8 argues theoretically that |V|≫d forces shared feature directions. No empirical test of capacity competition or dedicated dimensions for important features.
No test of features being distributed across neurons. SAE quality (reconstruction, sparsity, interpretability) is not reported.
No test of completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, or canonicity of SAE features.
Directional invariance is assumed, with a theoretical bound only for binary features. The authors state they do not characterize 1-D versus higher-dimensional subspaces.

missing.what: Head-level alignment percentages from the token-alignment validation (no row; linear-representation result, not V4)

Shared top-k SAE latent overlap for other datasets and models (Apple/Orange in LLaMA3-8B, Apple/Microsoft in Mistral, Fear/Shame in GPT-2). Shown only as figures without numbers; the text claims the pattern holds across datasets and model sizes.
Chance-level and Text Output baselines for the SAE accuracies
missing.locator: Table 1 class counts; Table 2 Text Output rows

record.verdict_notes: V4 evidence is indirect: classification from SAE latents shows that class information survives the SAE encoding, not that features are sparse or monosemantic. All Table 2 values are the best of many heads with no uncertainty estimates. Table 1 lists 6 author classes but App. D.1 lists 7 authors. Figure 3's caption and the text give different head percentages. The paper's 'superposition' wording for 'Apple' concerns token polysemy. Preprint, not peer reviewed.

versions.untested_parts: No test of sparse overcomplete toy networks storing features as nearly orthogonal overlapping directions, sparsity transitions, or regular superposition geometry.
No test that neuron polysemanticity is caused by capacity competition, that important features get dedicated dimensions, or that less important features share them.
The paper does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
Tests SAE-based recovery of semantic task information and token-instance SAE-feature overlap, but not whether features are broadly distributed across neurons.
Does not establish SAE features as complete, stable, or canonical units; it reports task classification and feature overlap.
Does not compare one-dimensional with multidimensional feature representations or determine when invariant subspaces are one-dimensional.

rows.subject: 2-layer transformer
rows.stage_stated: trained on modular division with p = 97
rows.operation_detail: Train with an MLP classification head instead of a standard linear unembedding.
rows.measure: Validation accuracy; separately trained linear-probe accuracy; Fourier geometry
rows.value: MLP head ∼95% validation accuracy; linear probe ∼20%; embeddings lacked circular structure
rows.note: This concerns whether a nonlinear readout allows alternatives to Fourier structure; it does not test the listed superposition versions.

rows.subject: 2-layer transformer

rows.operation_detail: Across random seeds, relate emergence of Fourier structure to linear-probe success.
rows.value: Runs developing Fourier structure also had successful linear probes
rows.note: The paper reports this correlation without giving a numeric result for those runs.

relationships.condition: SAEs on attention-head outputs of LLaMA3-8B, Llama3.2-3B and Mistral-7B; class-token/instance latent overlap in LLaMA3-8B Animals
relationships.reason: SAE latents trained without class tokens classify well above chance on most tasks (r01–r05, r07–r13, r15–r21, r23–r24). Class tokens share 15–25 of their top-32 latents with instances (r33–r36).
relationships.display_finding: SAE latents trained without class tokens classified well above chance on most tasks, and in the LLaMA3-8B Animals task class tokens shared 15–25 of their top-32 latents with instances.

relationships.condition: GPT2-Small SAEs, and the Emotions task in all models
relationships.reason: GPT2-Small SAE accuracy is near chance on C. Chars, Authors and Emotions (r27, r28, r30) and only modestly above chance on Animals, Countries and Fruits (r25, r26, r31). Companies (r32) is about double chance, and only Languages (r29) is strong. Emotions is weak in every model (r06, r14, r22).
relationships.display_finding: GPT2-Small SAE accuracy was near chance on C. Chars, Authors and Emotions and only modestly above chance on Animals, Countries and Fruits. Companies reached about double chance, only Languages was strong, and Emotions was weak in every model.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
